payload.author: Juan Lentino
payload.content:
A signature seals whatever it is given, and it seals the date with the same fidelity it seals everything else: exactly as written. Which is the problem, because the signer writes the date. Every other field in a signed record describes something the mathematics can check against the content. The time field describes something only a clock witnessed, and the signer owns the clock.

Self-reported time, sealed

What an in-record date amounts to is a self-report that cannot be edited later. That is worth something: the signer is bound to the claim, and changing it afterward breaks the seal. What it is not worth is priority. In music, time carries a disproportionate share of the argument. Who wrote it first, whether a recording predates the model that supposedly produced it, when a term began running, which of two claims to one melody came earlier: the hard questions are time questions. A field the claimant fills in unsupervised settles none of them, no matter how well it is sealed.

The failure is invisible in the demo and decisive in the dispute. A verifier shows the date in green beside the valid signature, and nothing on the screen distinguishes a witnessed time from an asserted one. The two records look identical at every point except the one where somebody asks what stood behind the clock.

An anchor proves no later than, never no earlier

An anchor is a commitment of the record to a clock the signer does not control, and the first thing to understand is which direction it points. An anchor proves the record existed no later than a moment. It proves nothing about no earlier. A record written in 2026 can claim a 1995 session and be anchored honestly the day it is written; the anchor will say existed by 2026, which contradicts nothing and confirms nothing. Anchors bound claims from one side only.

That one-sidedness makes the gap between the claimed date and the anchor date a signal in its own right, and it may be the most useful reading an anchored record offers. A session claimed in March and anchored in March is a tight claim, with days of room for invention. The same session anchored three years later carries three years in which the story could have been composed. Nothing forbids the loose claim. The record simply wears its looseness where a dispute can see it.

Music's disputes favor the coarse clock nobody owns

The replacement clock has to belong to somebody, and the two available answers split on a familiar axis. A timestamping authority, a third party whose business is signing the pair of a record's fingerprint and the current time, offers precision down to the second and asks for trust in return: its clock, its honesty, its answerability to whoever can compel it, and its continued existence on the day verification is needed. A public chain offers the opposite trade. Nobody owns its ordering, and its precision is coarse, hours or a day rather than seconds.

A · Timestamping authority

Precise, and owned

Fixes the time to the second. Asks for trust in its clock, its honesty, and its survival.

B · Public chain

Coarse, and ownerless

Fixes the time to within hours or a day. Nobody owns the ordering, and no single company has to last.

Neither choice removes trust from the system, since trust under these designs relocates rather than disappears. For music the trade still tilts hard toward the coarse, ownerless clock, because music's time disputes argue in years, not seconds, and catalogs outlive companies. A dispute over a 2026 session will be argued in 2036, and an authority's continued existence across that decade is a bet, while a widely replicated public ledger is a smaller one.

The empirical situation is stranger than the design question. The common configuration in the field is the weakest one available: signatures with no anchor at all, which makes the records sealed self-reports and leaves every date in them exactly as strong as its signer's word. The strengthening exists and costs nearly nothing. That it mostly goes unused says the field has not yet met the dispute that will teach it to care.

References

Adams, C., Cain, P., Pinkas, D., and Zuccherato, R. "Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure Time-Stamp Protocol (TSP)." RFC 3161, August 2001. rfc-editor.org

OpenTimestamps. "A timestamping proof standard." Accessed October 2026. opentimestamps.org

Todd, P. "OpenTimestamps: Scalable, Trust-Minimized, Distributed Timestamping with Bitcoin." September 15, 2016. petertodd.org
payload.title: The clock is the weak part
